And so that was that moment on the flight walking into the to the bathroom cabin and seeing your product there is just unreal. No words. You're just like, "Holy shit." >> Makes sense. You guys are remote. I mean, rumor has it you may or may not have sold for over $500 million. You have said that you've done 165 million plus fully remote. How is that even possible like at that type of scale? Like what are those big things that you do to keep efficiencies remotely? >> I try to find people who thrive in a remote setting. And when you talk about people who have sort of no distinction between work and life, it's they're just not that they have to work all the time, but they're just trying to achieve excellence in their life no matter what, right? They have a sense of pride for their career and the brand they're working with. It's like a doer, right? Like the type of person that's just they're not going to rest if the dishes aren't done. And it's like it's a personality, you know, and you either have it or you don't. So, it's like you can't you can write these like culture things like of like what people should be, but I find that kind of useless. You just you look for personalities that are just like selfstarters, people who want to be remote, not because they get to walk their dog or whatever. It's because they're more efficient and they care about what they're doing and they want to build something meaningful. Those people exist. They're harder to find and when you get them, you got to keep them. And so building an organi or organization the at least the goal is try to have everybody have that personality. So you meet somebody with the track record that they're with soand so brand that's just massive and they've done this done that and you meet them and you just feel like you know what maybe this person is not going to be great remote, right? And they're not going to thrive in a remote setting and so you have to pass on them. And so just making sure that everyone is is got that built into them. And then from a leadership perspective, finding people who are like many founders, like many CEOs of their own category, right? And so it makes the hiring process hard. One thing we do have going for us is we are remote. So people value that. the people who actually value remote work will will prioritize that and and and come work for us rather than have to go sit in an office and drive 30 minutes there and 30 minutes back or whatever it is. >> Opens up the pool for for more people to come. >> That's right. You find amazing talent anywhere. You could find talent in the Midwest or wherever and you're not limited by oh well our office is in New York City so we have to find somebody who can commute in. What do those many CEOs look like and how does that kind of ladder up to you? >> So, I work closely with them. I mean, I have one-on- ones with a couple of them who've wanted to keep it, but I talk with them so much. Like, my CMO, there's just like it feels like every hour we're we're pinging each other for something, jumping on, jumping off, and it's like, why would we set a one-on-one for somebody I'm talking to all the time anyways? So, I'd say the most successful people at Salt and Stone have that kind of relationship with me that are just always hitting me up. I'm always hitting them up. It's not like, "Okay, let's let's meet once a week and talk about how your week went." And so, it's like, "You're in it. We're in it together. We're going to be communicating." >> These are good problems, man. These are all these all sound like really, really good problems. You guys use recruiters? How do you how are you getting all this talent? I mean, obviously, you have a great brand that people want to work for, but there is there any kind of hiring tactics and tricks that you've used? >> We started using recruiters not that long ago. I [snorts] was spending a lot of time on LinkedIn. A lot of our our best employees have come from me scouting them out on LinkedIn, sending them a message, especially as the brand got bigger. They would reply and I'd get meetings with them and we'd be able to successfully hire them. So, I spent a lot of time, hours every single day on LinkedIn looking at different talent, just playing that like sports team GM role, you know what I mean? Like I got to find my all-star here, my all-star there. How are they going to work together? And so, I found I had a lot of fun with it, but ultimately it takes a lot of time. I will do it now. If if somebody has to leave or we're we're hiring for something new and meaningful, I I will spend hours on LinkedIn and try to find top talent. >> Yeah. One of my buddies like that was like he scaled a company to nine figures and that was like what he spent most of his time on. And looking back, I always thought he was crazy, but that's like a very like a very good usage of your time. It's just talent acquisition. >> Talent acquisition. >> That's right. I'm a I'm basically a recruiter, right? Like you're only as good as your team. So, what else are you going to spend your time on at this point? You got the beautiful perfect product. You got all these things going and now if somebody leaves, it should be a priority for you to find the A+ player, the Michael Jordan of of whatever that category is. >> When I look at you, I feel like you've obviously, especially in the beginning when it was like just you and a couple people, like you were doing every single role. But when I look at you, I think you're a highly creative individual. You're a brand guy, a visionary I would say. And when you like look at the book is a great book. It's called Rocket Fuel. There's a visionary and then there's an integrator. There's probably a lot of people out there listening that are like almost creative and brand people first and they're kind of thrown into this CEO role. Like you literally came like snowboarding kind of a smaller business and then you're thrust into this massive company. What's your advice that you would give to kind of these creative first leaders? I would say trust your instincts and if you feel like you have an idea and you feel like you are a visionary, trust it. And then you get thrown into having to do a lot of different things and wear a lot of different hats and you just have no option but to learn these things and figure them out. And I think that that comes back to having the passion for what you're doing because if you truly hate it or just can't figure it out or don't want to figure it out, you're going to have to hire help. you can't do what I did whereas like I ran this thing all by myself for the first three years. So it it's hard. My advice it's it's not so much advice. It's like hopefully as a founder you have that passion. Hopefully you have that thing that eats away at you that you're just like cannot sleep because you want this thing to be so successful. And I think you either have it or you don't. Brutal but true. What were those key hires though? Cuz I'm sure there was a moment where you're like, "Okay, this thing is scaling fast. I need to get in more people. When you look back at this journey, who what were those big inflection points of the hires that ultimately freed up your time and allowed you to kind of help scale the company? Yeah, my my first hire was comes to mind. You know, I I was doing everything. All the ops, the shipping, like everything, the ordering, you know, to the manufacturer, finding suppliers, AR, like collecting payments from retailers, every little piece of the brand. >> Those are the good old days, baby. >> I mean, man, it was so fun. You know, I don't talk about it like, man, that sucked. It was just so fun building something, seeing it come to life. Like, what's better than that? What else are you going to do? >> Dude, I remember the first couple million and just working till my face was burnt off and then sleeping on bean bags and no weekdays, no weekends. I still put in the work, but especially if it's working. If it's working and you're doing it by yourself and you're doing everything and and all you're doing is work. I didn't have a family at that point either, you know. I had a girlfriend, but I didn't have kids, you know. So, I could just go relentlessly like all the time. And when it's working out and you know the brand is growing and it's this thing, it's your first time doing something on your own other than pro snowboarding like it's so fun, man. It's the best. It's what you live for. >> Yeah. You said something there that I think is like for anybody out there listening like you have to find a way to put yourself in a spot where the efforts of your input directly tied to the output. Like I just remember it was like the harder I worked the luckier I got. The harder I worked the more money I made. And that was like the beginning. Um and I just remember it's just like there was just not enough hours in the day. And I just wanted to work every day all day because I just saw direct benefit. And I think you have to find that. >> You do. I mean, and look, half of the thing is just going for it is being a doer, you know, and that's why being a doer will always outperform a thinker. You know, someone who's just gonna, you know, just sit there and dwell on it and write their ideas down and and you know, is this calculate? Like, you have an idea, you just got to go. That's those are the type of people who are successful. And if that doesn't work, you just do it again over and over again, you know, and and something will work. cards.title: Screen for remote-work self-starters
cards.claim: A Salt and Stone leader says the company prioritizes people who thrive remotely, are self-starters, and care about building something meaningful.
cards.action: When hiring for a remote organization, pass on candidates who do not seem likely to thrive in a remote setting, even if their track record is strong.
applies_when: Assessing candidates beyond prior brand pedigree
unknowns: No interview rubric or validation method is provided.
No retention or performance outcomes are provided.
evidence_quotes: I try to find people who thrive in a remote setting.

You just you look for personalities that are just like selfstarters, people who want to be remote, not because they get to walk their dog or whatever. It's because they're more efficient and they care about what they're doing and they want to build something meaningful.
you meet them and you just feel like you know what maybe this person is not going to be great remote, right? And they're not going to thrive in a remote setting and so you have to pass on them.

cards.title: Founder-led LinkedIn talent scouting
cards.claim: The speaker reports sourcing many of the company's best employees through direct LinkedIn outreach before using recruiters.
cards.action: For a new or meaningful hire, spend time on LinkedIn identifying top talent and sending direct messages.
applies_when: Hiring for something new and meaningful
A founder or leader can personally source candidates
unknowns: The passage does not provide response rates, hiring conversion, or time-to-fill.
The proportion of hires sourced through recruiters versus LinkedIn is not provided.
evidence_quotes: We started using recruiters not that long ago.
A lot of our our best employees have come from me scouting them out on LinkedIn, sending them a message, especially as the brand got bigger.
If if somebody has to leave or we're we're hiring for something new and meaningful, I I will spend hours on LinkedIn and try to find top talent.

cards.title: Use frequent ad hoc communication with key leaders
cards.claim: The speaker says their most successful Salt and Stone leaders communicate continuously rather than relying on a weekly one-on-one.
cards.action: For leaders you already communicate with frequently, use ongoing pings and short check-ins rather than setting a weekly meeting solely to review the week.
applies_when: Working closely with key functional leaders
unknowns: The passage does not establish that this approach works for every role or team.
No communication tools, cadence standards, or decision-rights process is specified.
evidence_quotes: Like, my CMO, there's just like it feels like every hour we're we're pinging each other for something, jumping on, jumping off, and it's like, why would we set a one-on-one for somebody I'm talking to all the time anyways?
I'd say the most successful people at Salt and Stone have that kind of relationship with me that are just always hitting me up. I'm always hitting them up.
It's not like, "Okay, let's let's meet once a week and talk about how your week went."
